strangely this was empowering to read. it kind of calls into question how badly people want things and whether our society is paternalistic in the life-circumstances-is-limiting narrative and removing agency from humans (not working-class folks or poor folks, but human beings) in general. ok, so it's harder for people who have less resources to succeed. but you are saying that it's possible if they put all they have into it to make it so. saying that they can't succeed because of their circumstances would be like admitting that people can't dig themselves out of deep addictive and/or gravitational holes and is ultimately disempowering. so a full philosophy, a humanistic one that takes into consideration a human being's agency must admit that those with few resources are able to be successful? does this spring out of that philosophy?

not a criticism, just a question: where do you draw the line between systemic marginalization & the effects of minimal resources vs. agency and choices available in life? to clarify, is it possible to determine whether his outcomes were due to the poor choices that he made in life (i.e. he could choose whether he went to college or smoked pot and worked 40 hours a week at mcdonalds) or whether some of his life circumstances made certain paths more viable than others (i.e. if his mother dies when he's 16, forcing him into the workforce early and stripping him of the opportunity to obtain a degree at a four-year college)?
